senses: dignitary (a person of high rank, a person in high office)
la:noun:dignitas.html:
dignĭtas, ātis (
gen. plur. dignitatum, ; ; : -tatium,), f.
dignus
.
Lit., a being worthy, worth, worthiness, merit, desert (so, rarely, and perh. only in Cic.): Lamia petit praeturam: omnesque intelligunt nec dignitatem ei deesse nec gratiam,; id. Agr.

2, 2, 3: dignitas consularis,a being worthy of the office of consul,: pro dignitate laudare,.

Meton. (the cause for the effect), dignity, greatness, grandeur, authority, rank (cf. honos, honestas, laus, existimatio, gloria, fama, nomen).
In gen.: mihi gratulabere, quod audisses me pristinam meam dignitatem obtinere. Ego autem, si dignitas est bene de re publica sentire, obtineo dignitatem meam; sin autem in eo dignitas est, si, quod sentias, re efficere possis, ne vestigium quidem ullum est reliquum nobis dignitatis,; dignitas (est) alicujus honesta et cultu et honore et verecundia digna auctoritas,: cum pulchritudinis duo genera sint, quorum in altero venustas est, in altero dignitas; venustatem muliebrem ducere debemus, dignitatem virilem,: formae,; : corporis, Laber. ap. ; ; cf. also ; ; : agere cum dignitate ac venustate,: personarum dignitas, § 141: retinere in rebus asperis dignitatem,: in senatu conservanda auctoritas, apud populum dignitas, et saep.: celsissima sedes dignitatis atque honoris,: ex tam alto dignitatis gradu,; cf. (twice): est in ipsis (liberis populis) magnus delectus hominum et dignitatum,: aliquem ex humili loco ad summam dignitatem perducere,: aliquem dignitate exaequare,: ut secundum locum dignitatis Remi obtinerent,; ; cf. ; 7, 66, 5; 7, 77, 6; et saep.—
In partic.
Official dignity, honorable employment, office: gratulor laetorque tum praesenti tum etiam sperata tua dignitate,; id. ap. ; cf. in plur., ; —
Men holding high office, men in honorable employment: cum dignitates abessent,; cf. .—
Transf., of inanimate things, worth, value, excellence: opsonii,: praeclara et plena dignitatis domus,; cf. porticus,; : portus, urbis,: loci,: dignitas, quae est in latitudine pectoris,: verborum,; ; cf. : debita rerum,; cf. : subsequendi,: cum dignitate actionis,

la:adj:dignus.gloss: appropriate, fitting, worthy, meet, deserving, fit, proper, suitable, becoming
senses: appropriate, fitting, worthy, meet, deserving, fit, proper, suitable, becoming
la:adj:dignus.html:
dignus, a, um, adj.
i. e. DIC-nus; root in Sanscr. daç-as, fame; Gr. δοκέω, δόξα; Lat.: decet, decus
,
worthy, deserving (in a good or ill sense), of things, suitable, fitting, becoming, proper (very freq. in all periods and kinds of writing).—Constr., in the most finished models of composition, with the abl. pretii, a relative sentence, or absol.; in the Aug. poets also freq. with the inf.; otherwise with ut, the gen., or the acc. of a neutr. pron. or adj.
With abl. (so most freq.): dignus domino servus,; cf.: vir patre, avo, majoribus suis dignissimus,; ; juvenes patre digni, et saep.: dignus es verberibus multis,: amici novi digni amicitiā,: summa laude digni,; et saep.: omnibus probris, quae improbis viris Digna sunt, dignior nullus est homo,: assentatio, quae non modo amico, sed ne libero quidem digna est,; : dignius odio scelus,: o fons, dulci digne mero,: munera digna venustissima Venere,; for which; diem dignum Veneri (abl. v. Venus), : ut te dignam mala malam aetatem exigas,; cf. ; et saep.: dicendum dignum aliquid horum auribus,: aliquid memoria dignum consequi,; * ; : si quid antea admisissem piaculo dignum, et saep.: tribuere id cuique, quod sit quoque dignum,: neque enim decorum est neque dis dignum,: quicquid dignum sapiente bonoque, et saep.: dicere Cinnā digna,.—Esp. freq. with supine in u: digna memoratu produntur,: nihil dignum dictu,; ; ; ; ; ; .—
With rel. clause (freq., though not in the Aug. poets): non videre dignus, qui liber sies,; cf. ; : qui modeste paret, videtur, qui aliquando imperet, dignus esse,: homines dignos, quibuscum disseratur putant,; et saep.—So with rel. adv.: sive adeo digna res est ubi tu nervos intendas tuos,if the thing is really worth your bending your energies to it,; cf. also: dignos esse, qui armis cepissent, eorum urbem agrumque Bolanum esse, i. e. ut eorum urbs esset, Weissenb. (Madv. dignum, cf. δ infra).—
Absol. (that of which some one or something is worthy, to be supplied from the context): Mi. Quem ament igitur? Sy. Alium quemlibet; Nam nostrorum nemo dignus est (sc. amari),; cf. : ut ne nimis cito diligere incipiant neve non dignos, etc.,: illud exemplum ab dignis et idoneis ad indignos et non idoneos transfertur, Kritz.: dignis ait esse paratus,: omnes, ait, malle laudatos a se, dignos indignosque, quam, etc., et saep.: quem dices digniorem esse hominem hodie Athenis alterum?; cf. : dignus patronus,: dignior heres, Hor. C. 2, 14, 25: digna causa,: dignum operae pretium,: dignas grates persolvere,; : digna gloria ruris, et saep.: ad tuam formam illa digna est,; so, quod supplicium dignum libidini ejus invenias? (where the dat. depends on the verb), : id, cum ipse per se dignus putaretur, impetravit,.—So as subst.: "nulla contumelia est, quam facit dignus;" primum quid est dignus? nam etiam malo multi digni, sicut ipse (Antonius), ; so, dignum est, it is fit, proper, becoming, = aequum est, decet, convenit, ; ; ; ; ; ; Sen. de Ira, 1, 12; —So comp., ; .—Sup., .—
With inf. (freq. in the Aug. poets; not in Cic.): concedere,: unā perire,: credere,: fuisse conjux,: decurrere spatium vitae,: ponere annos, al.; and more freq. in the pass.: cantari dignus,: amari,: rapi,: describi,: notari,: legi,: et saep.: auctoribus hoc dedi, quibus dignius credi est,; cf.: uterque optimus erat, dignusque alter elegi, alter eligere,.—(ε) With ut: non sum dignus prae te, ut figam palum in parietem,; : eras dignus ut haberes integram manum; ; .—(ζ) With gen. (acc. to the Gr. ἄξιός τινος—so freq. in Inscr. v. Wordsworth, Fragm. p. 494): dignus salutis,; cogitatio dignissima tuae virtutis, Balb. ap. A.: quidquid putabit dignum esse memoriae,: probae,.—(η) With acc. of a neutr. pron. or adj.: non me censes scire quid dignus siem?; : si exoptem, quantum dignus, tantum dent (di tibi), etc.,.—(θ) With ad (very rare): ad tuam formam illa una digna est,: amicus, dignus huic ad imitandum,.—(ι) With pro: si digna poena pro factis eorum reperitur,; ; .—Adv.: dignē, worthily, fitly, becomingly: quam digne ornata incedit, haud meretricie!; ; ; Cassius in ; ; ; ; —Comp., .—Sup. seems not to occur.

digno, āre, 1, v. a.
dignus
,

la:adj:dignissimus.gloss: appropriate, fitting, worthy, meet, deserving, fit, proper, suitable, becoming

senses: to deign, think something worthy of oneself (to do)
la:verb:dignor.html:
dignor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. a. [dignus], to deem worthy or deserving (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Aliquem aliqua re: haud equidem tali me dignor honore,; so, aliquem honore,; ; al.: te alio funere,: hunc mensa, cubili (dea),: aliquem non sermone, non visu,: libellum veniā,; —
With inf. as object, like the Gr. ἀξιῶ and ἀξιοῦμαι, to regard as fit, becoming, worthy of one's self, to deign; and with a negative, not to deign, to disdain: jam nemo suspicere in caeli dignatur lucida templa,; so with a neg., * ; ; ; 464; ; ; ; —Affirmatively: quos eximia specie donare natura dignata est,: cui se pulcra viro dignetur jungere Dido,; ; ; ; ; 7; : si digneris audire,.—
With double acc.: o felix si quem dignabitur, inquit, ista virum,will hold worthy to be her husband,; so, regem nostrum filium,.—
Ellipt. with one acc. (the inf. to be supplied from the context): orant succedere muris Dignarique domos (sc. visere),: nullo Macedonum dignante Parthorum imperium,.—Hence, dignanter, adv., courteously, with complaisance (post-class. and very rare): loquentem dignanter audite,: impertire,.— Sup. Auct. Itin. Alex. 10.

la:verb:digero.html:
dī-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3,
v. a., to force apart, separate, divide, distribute (cf.: dispono, distribuo, divido, dispenso, ordino, compono).
Lit.
Ingen. (so mostly post-Aug.): (insulae) interdum discordantibus ventis digeruntur (opp. junctae copulataeque),; cf. nubes (opp. congregare),: nimbos,; : digesti colores,: stercoris pars in prata digerenda,: radix digesta,: inque canes totidem trunco digestus ab uno Cerberus,divided, separated,; cf.: Nilus

septem in cornua, (for which, septem discretus in ostia Nilus, ): Crete centum per urbes,: populus Romanus in classes (coupled with distributus), et saep.; cf. .—Poet.: (augur Thestorides) novem volucres in belli digerit annos,i. e. explains, interprets, (cf. omina, ).—

In partic.
(Post-Aug.): cibum, to cut up, divide: (dentes) qui digerunt cibum,; and still more freq., like the class. concoquere,to digest, prooem.; ; ; —
In medic. lang., to dissolve, dissipate morbid matter, (twice); 1, 9 fin.; 2, 17 al.; — Very freq. and class.,
With the accessory notion of arrangement, to distribute, arrange, dispose, set in order: quas (accepti tabulas) diligentissime legi et digessi,; cf. : capillos,: crines, Col. poet. 10, 165; cf.: crines ordine,: asparagum,to plant in regular rows,; ; cf. and 267: bibliothecam,to arrange,: carmina in numerum, (ordinat, disponit, Serv.).
Trop.
In gen., to distribute (rare and not ante-Aug.): quam meruit solus poenam digessit in omnes,; cf.: mala per annos longos,: tempora,; cf.: annum in totidem species, et saep.—Freq. and class.,
In partic., to arrange, set in order, distribute: mandata,: quaestiones,; cf. Spald. N. cr.: reliquos usus ejus suo loco,to relate in order, et saep.: omina,interprets, (cf. above, no. I. A. fin.): post descripte et electe in genus quodque causae, quid cuique conveniat, ex hac copia digeremus,; cf. : omne jus civile in genera,: commentarios in libros,: res in ordinem, prooem. § 1: argumenta in digitos,: commentarium per genera usus sui, et saep.—With a relat. clause: nec quid quoque anno actum sit, in tanta vetustate non modo rerum sed etiam auctorum digerere possis,: senium, digest, i. e. endure, (cf. γῆρας ἕψειν, Pind. Olym. 1, 133).—
To consider maturely (late Lat.): consilium,; .—
To exercise (for health): si satis valet, gestando aegrum, digerere; si parum, intra domum tamen dimovere,: ne imbecillum hominem nimis digerant, al.—Hence, dīgestus, a, um, P. a.
(Acc. to I. B. 1.) That has a good digestion: purissimus et digestissimus, Marc. Empir. c. 22 med.—
(Acc. to no. II. B.) Subst.: dīgesta, ōrum, n., a name given to a collection of writings distributed under certain heads, ; esp. of Justinian's code of laws, the Pandects, Digests; cf. .—Also to the Bible, .—Sing.: digestum Lucae,the Gospel of Luke,.

dīgressus, ūs, m.
digredior
,

la:verb:digredior.gloss: to go apart or asunder, separate, part; go away, depart
senses: to go apart or asunder, separate, part; go away, depart
la:verb:digredior.html:
dī-grĕdĭor, gressus, 3,
v. dep. n. [gradior], to go apart or asunder, to separate, part; to go away, depart, = discedere (class.).
Lit.: luna tum congrediens cum sole, tum digrediens,; cf.: digredimur paulum rursumque ad bella coimus,: ita utrique digrediuntur,; cf.: digredimur flentes,: ubi digressi,.—With term. a quo: numquam est a me digressus,: ab aliquo,; ; ; ; ; ; cf.: a marito,to abandon,: a colloquio Caninii,; : a Corcyra,: ex eo loco,; cf.: ex colloquio,: domo,: triclinio,; cf. : inde, —Absol.: hos ego digrediens lacrimis affabar obortis,; cf. ; ; : dein statim digrediens,stepping aside, Kritz. —With term. ad quem: ambo in sua castra digressi,; ; ; cf.: in urbem ad capessendos magistratus,: ad sua tutanda,; : Seleuciam,: domum,: digredientem eum cum Caesare circumsistunt,.
Trop., to go aside, deviate, depart. —With term. a quo: nos nostro officio nihil digressos esse. * .—
Esp., in speaking or writing, to digress (but de-gredi, which is sometimes found in edd. in this sense is incorrect, v. h. v.): digredi ab eo, quod proposueris,: parumper a causa,

fin.: de causa,: ex eo et regredi in id,.—Absol.: saepe datur ad commovendos animos digrediendi locus,; so ; ; : verum huc longius, quam voluntas fuit, ab epistola Timarchidi digressa est oratio mea,: sed eo jam, unde huc digressi sumus, revertamur,; cf. ; .

senses: an inch (in ancient times, a 16th part of a Roman foot)
la:noun:digitus.html:
dĭgĭtus, i, m.
Gr. δάκτυλος; cf. Germ. Zehe, Eng. toe; from root δεκ(δέχομαι), to grasp, receive; cf. Germ. Finger, from fangen,. Corssen, however, still refers digitus to root dik-, dico, δείκνυμι, as the pointer, indicator, Ausspr. 1, 380; cf. dico
,
a finger.
Prop.: tot (cyathos bibimus), quot digiti sunt tibi in manu,; ; ; et saep.—The special designations: pollex, the thumb; index or salutaris, the forefinger; medius, also infamis and impudicus, the middle finger; minimo proximus or medicinalis, the ring-finger; minimus, the little finger, v. under those words.—
Special connections: attingere aliquem digito (uno),to touch one lightly, gently,; Ruhnk.; Licinius ap. ; ; cf. with tangere,; : attingere aliquid extremis digitis (with primoribus labris gustare),to touch lightly, to enjoy slightly,: attingere caelum digito,to be exceedingly happy,: colere summis digitis, to adore (to touch the offering or consecrated gift) with the tips of the fingers, ; fin.; cf. : computare digitis,to count on the fingers, to reckon up,; , no. 29, § 88; cf.: numerare per digitos,: in digitis suis singulas partis causae constituere,.—Hence, venire ad digitos, to be reckoned, ; and: si tuos digitos novi,thy skill in reckoning,; cf. also: digerere argumenta in digitos,to count on the fingers,: concrepare digitos or digitis, to snap the fingers, as a signal of command, ; ; ; v. concrepo; cf. also: digitus crepans,: digitorum crepitus,: digitorum percussio,: intendere digitum ad aliquid,to point the finger at any thing,: liceri digito,to hold up the finger in bidding at an auction,; for which also: tollere digitum,. The latter phrase also signifies, to raise the finger in token of submission, said of a combatant, ; cf. ; and Schol,: loqui digitis nutuque,to talk by signs,; different is: postquam fuerant digiti cum voce locuti,i. e. playing as an accompaniment to singing,; cf.: ad digiti sonum,; cf. also ; : digito compesce labellum,hold your tongue,.—For the various modes of employing the fingers in oratorical delivery, cf. ; sq.; 103; 120 al.: monstrari digito, i. e. to be pointed out, to become distinguished, famous, ; ; for which: demonstrari digito,; ; ; ; .—Prov. phrases: nescit, quot digitos habeat in manu, of one who knows nothing at all,: in digitis hodie percoquam quod ceperit,i. e. he has caught nothing,: ne digitum quidem porrigere, not to stretch out a finger, like the Gr. δάκτυλον μὴ προτεῖναι, ἐκτεῖναι, for not to give one's self the least trouble, ; cf.: exserere digitum, Scal.; and in like manner: proferre digitum,to move a finger, to make any exertion,: scalpere caput digito, of effeminate men fearful of disarranging their hair,; cf. ; a habit of Pompey's, acc. to Calvus ap. Schol. , and ; . (Cf. Echtermeyer's Ueber Namen und symbolische Bedeutung der Finger bei den Griechen und Römern, Progr. d. Hall. Pädagogiums, v. 1835.)
Transf.
A toe (cf. Heb. , Gr. δάκτυλος, Fr. doigt), ; ; ; ; et saep.; also of the toes of animals, ; ; —
A small bough, a twig, ; .—
As a measure of length, an inch, the sixteenth part of a Roman foot (pes), ; ; ; : digiti primores, finger-ends, as a measure, ; digitus transversus,a fingerbreadth,fin.; 48, 2.—Prov.: digitum transversum non discedere ab aliqua re,not to swerve a finger's breadth,; cf. without transversum: nusquam ab argento digitum discedere,; and ellipt.: ab honestissima sententia digitum nusquam,.
